title: Creating tasks and choosing priorities

spans.text: LESSON PURPOSE

Goal: apply “Creating tasks and choosing priorities” to a real program or device. The key principle is: Each task consumes stack; priority affects scheduler choices. In a project, follow this guidance: An infinite task should block or wait periodically so it does not monopolize the CPU.
QUESTION: What will this example do? Predict the result first.
EXAMPLE CODE
EXPECTED RESULT
Serial Monitor prints fast task and slow task at their respective intervals.
CORE EXPLANATION
A task is a function with its own stack and execution context;
xTaskCreate
registers it with the scheduler. Set priority from a real timing need: an overactive high-priority task can starve lower-priority work. Arduino
loop()
is also an RTOS task, so plan shared access to Serial and peripherals.
IMPORTANT LINE BREAKDOWN
Key line:

void setup() { Serial.begin(115200); if (xTaskCreate(fastTask, "fast", 2048, nullptr, 1, nullptr) != pdPASS) Serial.println("fast task creation failed"); if (xTaskCreate(slowTask, "slow", 2048, nullptr, 1, nullptr) != pdPASS) Serial.println("slow task creation failed"); }

What it does: Each task consumes stack; priority affects scheduler choices.
Why it is used: An infinite task should block or wait periodically so it does not monopolize the CPU.
If omitted or changed: Serial output from multiple tasks may interleave; serialize shared output and measure stack use.
